definition: Brain technology, or self-learning know-how systems, defines a technology that employs latest findings in neuroscience.
details: [see also neuro implants] The term was first introduced by the Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in Zurich, Switzerland, in the context of the Roboy project. Brain Technology can be employed in robots, know-how management systems and any other application with self-learning capabilities. In particular, Brain Technology applications allow the visualization of the underlying learning architecture often coined as "know-how maps".

explainer.lead: Brain technology is a broad label for self-learning systems that draw on recent findings from neuroscience. It covers applications such as robots and know-how management systems, and includes “know-how maps” for visualizing how their learning architecture is organized.

tiers.eli5: Imagine building a robot that can learn, using ideas discovered by studying brains. Brain technology is the name for that general approach, whether the result is a robot or a system that organizes know-how. A know-how map is like a picture showing the parts involved in its learning.
tiers.practitioner: Treat brain technology as an application label rather than a ready-made algorithm: it applies neuroscience findings to self-learning robots, know-how management systems, and similar applications. Know-how maps can visualize the underlying learning architecture. The term does not prescribe a model, training method, or software stack, so those choices must be specified separately.
tiers.paperLevel: Brain technology, also called self-learning know-how systems, is defined as technology employing recent findings from neuroscience, particularly in applications with self-learning capabilities; know-how maps visualize the underlying learning architecture. The Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in Zurich, Switzerland, introduced the term in the context of the Roboy project. It does not identify a particular learning rule, architecture, or evaluation method.

explainer.example: In the Roboy context, brain technology describes a robot application built using neuroscience findings and capable of self-learning. Its learning architecture can be represented visually as a know-how map.

usedIn.detail: Self-learning know-how management systems can use the approach and visualize their learning architecture with know-how maps.

explainer.intuition: The central idea is to take current neuroscience findings into engineered systems that can learn for themselves. It is an umbrella concept for those applications, not the name of one specific technique.
howItWorks: Start with recent findings from neuroscience.
Apply those findings in a system designed to learn for itself.
Use the approach in a robot, a know-how management system, or another self-learning application.
Visualize the underlying learning architecture as a know-how map.
explainer.whyItMatters: It connects neuroscience research with practical self-learning systems and gives their learning architectures a visual representation. That visualization can make the organization of an application’s know-how easier to inspect.
misconceptions: Brain technology is not the name of a single algorithm or neural-network design.
Neuro implants are a related topic, but the term itself refers to self-learning technology informed by neuroscience.
A know-how map visualizes the learning architecture; it is not the learning system itself.
